newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish LOT mulls eurobond to fund expansion.
newsitem.headline: Polish LOT mulls eurobond to fund expansion.

text.p: Polish airline PLL LOT SA is considering an issue of up to $250 million in convertible eurobonds to increase its fleet by half, but the plan hinges on the firm's rapid privatisation, its president said on Friday.

Jan Litwinski told Reuters in an interview that without additional capital the company's development plans, which include the purchase of 13 Boeing aircraft by 2003 and an increase in the number of routes, will prove impossible. @
"We estimate the size of the issue at $200-250 million, from simulations conducted within the firm, while the exact scope of the privatisation will be determined by the adviser," Litwinski said.

Last year the transport minister cancelled the tender for a privatisation adviser for LOT, saying the costs were too high, but last Tuesday the government decided that a new tender would be announced shortly.
"If privatisation and an injection of capital does not come soon, LOT's development will be delayed," Litwinski said. @

He added that in 1997 LOT expected to get five Boeing aircraft, the leasing of which would cost $230 million. In 1999 to 2003 a further eight planes have been ordered but the value of the deal was not revealed.
LOT's deputy president Zbigniew Kiszczak said that purchase of those eight planes would not be possible without the airline's privatisation and significant capital injection.
Litwinski said the possible new issue would help the airline reduce leasing payments and thus improve the long-term financial situation of the company. @
"Our efforts to secure a capital injection are not aimed at improving our current financial position which is stable," he said.

Kiszczak said LOT recorded a 45.9 million zloty loss in 1996 after a modest 5.5 million profit in 1995 because a delay in expected capital increase prevented LOT from fully paying off some of its leased aircraft and thus reducing financial costs.

LOT, which carried 2.03 million passengers in 1996, up from 1.84 million in 1995, was originally earmarked for a partial sell-off in 1996, but now the sale of up to 49 percent of its shares is scheduled by mid-1998. @
Kiszczak, who is responsible for LOT's privatisation plans, said the airline's management would prefer to have financial investors and a dispersed shareholder structure to a single strategic partner.
"We are rather interested in neutral investors and dispersed shareholder structure," he said.

Kiszczak said LOT, which had code-sharing and marketing agrements with several carriers including American Airlines, Air France, Alitalia and Aeroflot, would not object to such partners taking relatively small minority stakes. @
"We do not rule out alliances in which a small number of LOT shares would be purchased by another airline but we would have to know exactly what its intentions would be," he added.
